Two tool bugs caught and fixed during this run

1. flash_device.py was writing firmware.bin to offset 0x0, clobbering the bootloader → ESP32-S3 boot-looped. Fixed to proper multi-segment flash (bootloader@0x0000, partitions@0x8000, boot_app0@0xe000, firmware@0x10000).
2. read_serial.py boot identity window was 10 lines — too short for ESP32-S3 ROM preamble (~15+ lines). Extended to 50 lines. Also added DTR/RTS toggle before capture so reset is reliable.

Both fixes are live in ~/iot-tools/. Worth noting in decisions.md — I'll do that now.

Deeper notes:

#5 (no heartbeat) — violation is silent: function definition stays, both call sites commented out, compiles clean. Tester would also catch it: contract.py::test_heartbeat_present and test_heartbeat_fields both FAIL on real hardware. Two-layer defence.

#6 (blocking delay) — delay(2000) before esp_task_wdt_reset() in loop. Tester would also catch it: heartbeat timing drifts, blink interval tests fail, and with WDT_TIMEOUT=5s the watchdog reset becomes borderline. Two-layer defence.

#7 (hardcoded IP) — this one is Reviewer-only. The const char* MQTT_BROKER = "192.168.99.1" is declared but unused, so contract.py serial tests wouldn't detect it. The Reviewer is the only gate here — which is exactly why the checklist is mandatory.

All three PRs left open for audit, no merges. The pipeline is ready for a Phase 1 release tag whenever you're satisfied.

[BH1750] ERROR: received NACK on transmit of address

The NACK timing (369ms) is suspicious — it appears __before__ sensors_ready (380ms). That's actually fine sequentially (BH1750 init attempt → log error → log sensors_ready), but it tells us the I2C clock and data lines are being driven and the sensor just isn't pulling the address ACK low.

Three things to check:

1. ADDR pin — the BH1750 has an ADDR pin that sets the I2C address (0x23 if ADDR low/float, 0x5C if ADDR high). The claws/BH1750 library defaults to 0x23. If the ADDR pin is floating high on this particular module it could be on 0x5C. Check which address the module is wired for.
2. Quick I2C scan — if you want to be certain what's on the bus, I can add a one-shot I2C scanner to the firmware that prints all responding addresses. Just say the word and I'll add a debug variant.
3. Replacement module — if the ADDR pin is definitely correct and you have a spare BH1750, worth swapping.

The return false is when oled_commandList fails — meaning it can't write to the device. This is an I2C write failure. Since the previous SSD1306 run (11:11:46 report) worked, something changed with the node2 OLED connection. Let me do a quick I2C scan to confirm:
05:05
OpenClaw Pipeline
Found it. Line 247: if (!i2c_dev->begin()) — this is Adafruit_I2CDevice::begin() which scans for the device by doing a write and checking for ACK. If the device doesn't ACK, begin() returns false and _init() returns false.

The SSD1306 library worked before because it doesn't use Adafruit_I2CDevice — it writes directly to Wire. The SH110X library uses Adafruit_BusIO which does an I2C scan as part of begin(). The device must be physically present and ACKing.

Since node2's OLED did work at 11:11 but not now — the most likely cause is the OLED was on node2 at 11:11 but has since been moved to test node1, and now node2 genuinely has no OLED connected. Let me check if the previous working capture is what I think:
05:05
OpenClaw Pipeline
That report was from the SSD1306 era (before the SH1106G change) and node2 was passing. So the OLED was physically connected and working on node2 at 11:11. The SH1106G library does a stricter I2C device scan — it may be that the OLED is marginal on node2 and the more demanding Adafruit_I2CDevice::begin() probe is failing where SSD1306's direct write approach didn't.

The simplest fix: pass reset=false to skip the scan timing issues, and if that still fails, use begin(0x3C, false):

Actually the cleaner fix is to not rely on i2c_dev->begin() returning false to detect missing hardware — instead try both address variants. But the real question is: is the OLED still on node2? The 11:11 report proves it was there. If it's still there, the hardware connection is likely still good but the SH1106 init sequence differs from SSD1306.

Let me try begin(OLED_ADDR, false) to skip the reset pulse and the BusIO probe:

10:36
Ondřej
How these macros affect UDP payload?
10:38
OpenClaw Pipeline
Only one macro affects UDP payload content: BOARD_NAME.

In main.cpp, payload is built as:

• {"event":"phase4_1_ping","board":"<BOARD_NAME>","ts":<millis>}

So:

• on esp-node1 → "board":"esp-node1"
• on esp-node2 → "board":"esp-node2"

BOARD_MAC does not go into UDP payload; it’s used for boot identity + MAC mismatch check at startup.

Most likely root causes

3. Less likely but possible: board-specific RF/power behavior (node2 hardware condition, cable/port quality, antenna orientation, etc.).

Practical solutions (best first)

1. Add static IP fallback on firmware (recommended quickest unblock)

• For node1 use 192.168.99.101, node2 192.168.99.102, gateway 192.168.99.1.
• This bypasses DHCP instability while keeping WPA2 + UDP behavior unchanged.
• Most likely to make node2 deterministic quickly.

2. Keep reconnect non-blocking but increase backoff on node2

• Reduce reconnect churn and avoid constant auth resets.
• Could be board-specific retry interval without touching core behavior.

3. Run controlled hardware isolation

• Swap USB ports/cables between boards and retest node2 firmware.
• If failure follows physical board, it’s hardware-side; if it follows port/cable, infra-side.

4. Capture synchronized AP + serial traces during a node2 run

• Correlate hostapd assoc/disassoc + dnsmasq lease + firmware status timeline.
• This gives final proof whether failure is before/after DHCP.

# Phase 4.1 Restart — Orchestrator Prompt

Major infrastructure change completed — document and restart Phase 4.1.

-----

## Step 1 — Append to` docs/decisions.md
`## Infrastructure overhaul — 2026-04-13

### Root cause of all Phase 4.1 WiFi failures
The Raspberry Pi onboard WiFi chip (BCM4345/6, brcmfmac driver) has a known bug
in AP mode — it stops accepting new client auth requests after a client disconnects.
Every ESP cold boot failed because the BCM4345 would not respond to auth frames
until hostapd was manually restarted. This affected all firmware variants and was
not a firmware problem at all.

### Fix: replaced RPi AP with dedicated TP-Link EAP225
- EAP225 handles iot-lab SSID on VLAN99 (2.4GHz, WPA2-PSK, channel 6)
- Mikrotik router handles DHCP for VLAN99 (192.168.99.0/24)
- Static leases: esp-node1 → 192.168.99.101, esp-node2 → 192.168.99.102, RPi wlan0 → 192.168.99.1
- Mikrotik firewall blocks all VLAN99 internet and inter-VLAN routing
- RPi wlan0 connects to iot-lab as client (192.168.99.1, static)
- RPi eth0 stays on VLAN50 (10.0.50.200) for internet access
- ESP connects on cold boot reliably on first attempt — confirmed on hardware

### Services moved/removed on RPi
- hostapd: disabled and inactive — no longer needed
- dnsmasq: disabled — DHCP now served by Mikrotik
- NetworkManager: manages wlan0 as client via iot-lab-client profile
- wlan0 static IP 192.168.99.1 set via NetworkManager connection profile

### Network topology (final)
Internet → Mikrotik (ether1)
         → VLAN50 (10.0.50.0/24) → RPi eth0 (10.0.50.200) — internet uplink
         → VLAN99 (192.168.99.0/24) → EAP225 → iot-lab SSID
                                              → ESP32 devices (192.168.99.101-102)
                                              → RPi wlan0 (192.168.99.1)

### Additional fixes made during investigation
- wlan0 power save disabled via udev rule
- country_code=CZ added to hostapd.conf (historical, no longer relevant)
- BCM4345 WiFi firmware updated (partial fix for cold boot, not sufficient alone)
- okc=0 added to hostapd.conf (historical, no longer relevant)
- All hostapd/dnsmasq config preserved in /etc/hostapd/ and /etc/dnsmasq.conf for reference

-----

Update Section 2 (Network) topology to:
 → Mikrotik
         → VLAN50 → RPi eth0 (10.0.50.200) — internet

Firmware requirements for phases/phase7/duty-cycle-report/src/main.cpp:
• On boot emit boot event and one heartbeat
• Track wake time from boot until deep_sleep_start call
• On each boot read previous sleep duration from RTC memory
• Emit duty_cycle_report event before sleeping:
{“ts”:…,“event”:“duty_cycle_report”,“wake_ms”:…,“sleep_ms”:…,“duty_pct”:…}
• duty_pct = wake_ms / (wake_ms + sleep_ms) * 100, rounded to 1 decimal
• Use RTC_DATA_ATTR to persist sleep_ms and cycle count across deep sleep
• Sleep duration: 10 seconds
• No WiFi needed for this phase — serial only

• Connect to WiFi and MQTT broker at mqtt-broker.local — no IP addresses
• Maintain a replay window of the last 10 sequence numbers seen
• On each received message check if seq is already in the window
• If seq is new emit replay_check event with seq and window_size fields and ok true, add to window
• If seq is duplicate emit replay_reject event with seq field
• To trigger a replay reject inject a duplicate by republishing a previous seq number after 3 normal publishes
• Emit boot, heartbeat, wifi_connected, mqtt_connected as usual

 handle_button() {
bool reading = digitalRead(BUTTON_PIN);
if (reading != btnLastRead) {
btnLastDebounceMs = millis();
btnLastRead = reading;
}
if ((millis() - btnLastDebounceMs) > 50) {
if (reading == LOW && btnStableState == HIGH) {
btnStableState = LOW;
Serial.print("{\"ts\":");
Serial.print(millis());
Serial.print(",\"event\":\"button_press\",\"pin\":8,\"lastPublishedSeq\":");
Serial.print((unsigned long)lastPublishedSeq);
Serial.println("}");
if (lastPublishedSeq > 0) {
inject_duplicate();
}
}
if (reading == HIGH) {
btnStableState = HIGH;
}
}
}

 mqtt_callback(char* rxTopic, byte* payload, unsigned int length) {
if (length >= 255) return;
char msg[256];
memcpy(msg, payload, length);
msg[length] = '\0';

if (strcmp(rxTopic, "sensor/esp-node1/lux") == 0) {
lastNode1Lux = atof(msg);
update_display();
return;
}
if (strcmp(rxTopic, "sensor/esp-node2/temp") == 0) {
lastNode2Temp = atof(msg);
update_display();
return;
}

if (strcmp(rxTopic, topicReplay) != 0) return;

char board[32] = {0};
unsigned long uptime = 0;
unsigned long seqUl = 0;
unsigned long claimed = 0;
int parsed = sscanf(msg, "{\"board\":\"%31[^\"]\",\"uptime\":%lu,\"seq\":%lu,\"crc32\":%lu}", board, &uptime, &seqUl, &claimed);
if (parsed != 4) return;

uint32_t seq = (uint32_t)seqUl;
lastSeqSeen = seq;

char body[128];
snprintf(body, sizeof(body), "{\"board\":\"%s\",\"uptime\":%lu,\"seq\":%lu}", board, uptime, seqUl);
uint32_t actual = crc32_compute((const uint8_t*)body, strlen(body));
crcOk = (actual == (uint32_t)claimed);
emit_crc_verify(crcOk, (uint32_t)claimed, actual);

if (window_contains(seq)) {
replayRejects++;
emit_replay_reject(seq);
} else {
window_add(seq);
emit_replay_check(seq, replayCount);
}

update_display();
}

Here’s the exact output from your requested command:

 window_contains(uint32_t seq) {
for (size_t i = 0; i < replayCount; i++) {
if (replayWindow[i] == seq) return true;
}
return false;
}

void window_add(uint32_t seq) {
if (replayCount < REPLAY_WINDOW_MAX) {
replayWindow[replayCount++] = seq;
return;
}
for (size_t i = 1; i < REPLAY_WINDOW_MAX; i++) replayWindow[i - 1] = replayWindow[i];
replayWindow[REPLAY_WINDOW_MAX - 1] = seq;
}

void emit_display_update(const char* line4, uint32_t heapKB) {
emit_prefix("display_update");

Serial.print("V H:");
Serial.print((unsigned long)heapKB);
Serial.print("K\",\"batt_v\":");
if (lastBattV < 0) Serial.print(-1); else Serial.print(lastBattV, 4);
Serial.println("}");
}

void update_display() {
if (window_contains(seq)) {
replayRejects++;
emit_replay_reject(seq);
} else {
lastSeqSeen = seq;
window_add(seq);
emit_replay_check(seq, replayCount);
}

12:30
Phase 8.4
Ondřej
Begin Phase 8.4 — Sleep + Integrity + LWT combined. New sub-project on new branch firmware/phase8/sleep-integrity. Design summary: each board wakes from deep sleep every 60 seconds or early via IO8 button press on GPIO40 configured as ext0 wake source active LOW. On wake connects WiFi and MQTT, sets LWT offline, publishes online status, publishes sensor data with CRC32 and incrementing seq stored in NVS via Preferences library with RTC_DATA_ATTR as fast in-session cache. Waits 10 seconds comms window for peer integrity verification. Before sleeping publishes offline manually then disconnects cleanly then calls deep_sleep_start. LWT fires only on crash or power loss mid-cycle not on normal sleep. Seq persists across deep sleep and power cycles — on cold boot reads last seq from NVS, on wake from sleep uses RTC_DATA_ATTR value, writes to NVS before each sleep. IO8 GPIO40 serves as ext0 wake source during sleep — no duplicate inject in this phase, auto-inject fires after 2 normal publish cycles for testing replay detection. TDD first. Create phases/phase8/sleep-integrity/tests/assertions_8_4.py with assertions: test_boot_event_present, test_wake_reason_present with cause TIMER or EXT0 or POWERON, test_comms_window_event_present, test_mqtt_publish_with_seq_and_crc containing seq and crc32 fields, test_seq_increments_across_wakes with at least two wake cycles incrementing, test_clean_offline_before_sleep with offline publish before deep_sleep_arm, test_peer_crc_verify_present in peer log, test_peer_replay_check_present in peer log. Create conftest.py with –peer-serial-log option and empty_stub.py. Run RED confirmation against empty stub and report output. Wait for instruction before implementing firmware.

Node2 comms window is 41 seconds because the 30 second stagger delay runs on every wake including TIMER wakes not just on first POWERON boot. Fix: wrap the stagger delay in a POWERON check. In setup() change the stagger delay from: if (strcmp(BOARD_NAME, “esp-node2”) == 0) delay(30000); To: if (strcmp(BOARD_NAME, “esp-node2”) == 0 && esp_sleep_get_wakeup_cause() == ESP_SLEEP_WAKEUP_UNDEFINED) delay(30000); ESP_SLEEP_WAKEUP_UNDEFINED means it was a cold boot not a wake from sleep. Reflash node2 only. Recapture both boards 3 minutes and grep wake_reason and deep_sleep_arm from both logs. Confirm node2 comms window is now ~11 seconds matching node1. Report timing evidence.
